name: Japanese beetle feeding injury
summary: A conspicuous adult beetle pest of hemp. Skeletonized leaves are compatible with feeding, but the metallic green-and-bronze adult and aggregated active feeding provide the strongest field evidence.
indicators: Metallic green adults with bronze wing covers are actively feeding on hemp
Leaf tissue between veins is consumed, leaving a lace-like or skeletonized appearance
Beetles may aggregate on exposed foliage or reproductive tissue
exclusions: No beetles are present and another defoliator is actively feeding
Damage is mined within leaf tissue rather than skeletonized from the surface
Skeletonization is old and no current infestation can be established

progression.description: Adults gather and chew exposed foliage or floral tissue.
Interveinal tissue is removed and veins remain as feeding intensifies.
Large aggregations can substantially reduce leaf area.

confirmation: Photograph adults with fresh damage and verify the characteristic adult morphology.
Do not assign Japanese beetle from skeletonization alone.
immediateActions: Count active beetles and estimate fresh defoliation rather than using cumulative old injury.
Scout nearby sun-exposed foliage and flowers.
correctivePlan: Use IPM appropriate to verified beetle pressure and locally legal hemp options.
prevention: Scout during seasonal adult emergence and record aggregation patterns.
Avoid assuming pheromone traps reduce damage; trapping can alter local beetle aggregation.
warnings: Skeletonization is not unique to Japanese beetle.
Economic thresholds established for other crops should not be copied directly to hemp without hemp-specific validation.

sources.title: Insect Pests of Industrial Hemp in Missouri
supportedClaims: Spotted cucumber beetle adults feed on hemp foliage and floral tissue, producing holes and ragged edges, while larvae can feed on root hairs and root tips.
Tarnished plant bug feeding on young hemp leaves, stems, buds, and flowers can produce chlorotic spots, leaf curling, terminal stunting, distorted buds, and bud abortion.
Dectes texanus larvae can bore inside hemp stems and pith, producing internal galleries, wilting, dieback, swollen or split stems, and increased breakage risk.
Cabbage looper larvae feed on hemp leaves, often from lower-leaf undersides upward, producing large irregular holes and potentially damaging floral buds.
Japanese beetle adults feed on hemp foliage and can skeletonize leaves between veins; adults are metallic green with bronze wing covers and often aggregate.
Armyworm larvae can create irregular holes and skeletonization and may enter hemp buds or flowers, where silk and frass can accompany feeding injury.
Hemp insect pressure varies by region, growth stage, and variety, so damage morphology without organism evidence should not be treated as species confirmation.
